doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

chapter: Discovering jazz and the trad band
title: Wartime childhood and the household's popular music
summary: American servicemen left no musical impression; his parents liked Mantovani and Doris Day and found his jazz strange.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did the American servicemen coming to England during the war have any impression on you, what they brought with them?
Of course you were only — not too old.

The only thing I can remember is that the favorite thing to do, if you saw American servicemen, was to go up to them and say, “Got any gum, chum?” And as kids, that’s what we did. That was about it. I can remember seeing American servicemen around but no awareness that they might have brought music or anything like that at all.
What was the music in your household like?
I think my father’s taste ran as far as Mantovani.
Yeah. Not too advanced, was it?
Well it was in my house too.

Yeah. They had their special musical interests at home. They just liked what they heard on the radio. Doris Day, Mantovani, Vera Lynn, you know, the kind of popular music — the popular music prior to the days of The Beatles and rock & roll if you like.
But they didn’t embrace any of the swing music that came over.
No. And when I got involved they thought it was a very strange thing altogether.
